raw_case_text:
Case report: A forty-three-year-old Sudanese male from Sennar State southeast Sudan presented to the urology clinic with milky urine for one year mainly at night and early morning, associated with lower urinary tract symptoms. There is no history of hematuria, back pain, trauma, or previous surgeries. However, he did mention that he had lost a significant weight during this time. Clinical examination revealed, a male of 170 cm, weighing 50 kg. Hemodynamically stable, with an unremarkable systemic examination.
Urine was milky in color, with two crosses of protein, triglyceride was 180 mg/d. 24 hours urine for Albumin was normal, serum cholesterol was normal, serum Albumin was 3.0 mg/dl, (CBC), kidney function, and liver function tests were all normal. Ether was added to a test tube filled with the cloudy urine rendering the mixture clear suggesting chyluria, A peripheral blood smear confirmed the presence of filarial parasites (Fig. 1). An abdominopelvic ultrasound and chest X-ray showed no abnormalities. Based on these findings, the patient underwent cystoscopy, and a milky white fluid was observed coming from the left ureteric opening during the procedure (Fig. 2).
We started first with a modification of dietary food and, anti-filariasis Ivermectin tablets 200 mug/Kg body weight for six days, this dose was repeated after 3 months, and after six months, but there was no improvement in his main complaint (milky urine). The patient consented to a retrograde pyelogram where a left pyelo-lymphatic fistula was confirmed (Fig. 3). As a result, sclerotherapy was initiated using povidone-iodine. A ureteral catheter was inserted, and a solution of 10 ml of 10 % povidone-iodine mixed with 10 ml of distilled water was prepared (this equals 20 ml of 5 % povidone Iodine). The solution was injected in a 10 ml syringe through the ureteral catheter, held for 5 minutes, and then released. This process was repeated until the full amount of the solution was administered. The treatment was administered three times daily for three consecutive days.
The patient was also treated with a third-generation cephalosporin (1 g twice daily) for three days of sclerotherapy and discharged on oral antibiotics Amoxicillin + clavulanic acid (1 gm twice daily for seven days) following the removal of the ureteral stent. There were no significant adverse effects during or after the procedure. The patient was seen two weeks following surgery and then monthly for one year. No recurrence of chyluria was observed during the follow-up period, and the patient reported no significant complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old Sudanese male presenting with a 1-year history of intermittent milky urine (predominantly nocturnal and early morning) accompanied by lower urinary tract symptoms and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the urology clinic with a 1-year history of passing milky-white urine, worse at night and early morning, associated with lower urinary tract symptoms and significant unintentional weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: From Sennar State, southeastern Sudan (filariasis-endemic region); no history of trauma or prior surgeries.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for milky urine (chyluria), lower urinary tract symptoms, and weight loss; negative for hematuria or back pain.

objective.physical_examination: Height 170 cm, weight 50 kg, hemodynamically stable, with an unremarkable systemic physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Macroscopically milky urine with 2+ proteinuria, elevated urinary triglycerides (180 mg/dL), normal 24-hour urinary albumin, and positive ether clearing test confirming chyluria. CBC, renal function, liver function tests, and serum cholesterol were normal; serum albumin was 3.0 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear confirmed filarial microfilariae. Abdominopelvic ultrasound and chest X-ray were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic cystoscopy demonstrated milky-white chylous efflux from the left ureteric orifice, and retrograde pyelography confirmed a left pyelo-lymphatic fistula.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed lymphatic filariasis complicated by chyluria secondary to a left pyelo-lymphatic fistula, established by peripheral blood smear microfilariae detection, cystoscopy, and retrograde pyelography.
Plan & Outcome: Initial dietary fat modification and three courses of oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg daily for 6 days at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months) failed to resolve chyluria. Subsequently underwent retrograde ureteral catheter instillation sclerotherapy with 5% povidone-iodine (three times daily for 3 days) under IV third-generation cephalosporin coverage (1 g twice daily), followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (1 g twice daily for 7 days). Achieved complete resolution of chyluria with no recurrence over 1 year of monthly follow-up.
